title: Given a string containing just the characters `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[` and `]`, determine if the input string is valid: brackets must be closed in the correct order by a matching pair.
shortTitle: Valid Parentheses: stack matching bracket pairs
keyPoints: Push every opener onto a stack; on each closer, pop and verify the top is the matching opener.
Return false immediately if the stack is empty when a closer arrives (unmatched close).
After the full scan, return stack.isEmpty() to catch unmatched openers like '((('.
A closer-to-opener Map keeps the matching logic clean and easy to extend.
Time is O(n) and space is O(n) worst case; each character is pushed and popped at most once.
Odd-length strings can never be balanced, so reject them in O(1) as a fast shortcut.

s1_definition.oneliner: Push every opener, and on every closer pop the top and check it matches; valid only if the stack ends empty.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Valid Parentheses** – verify that every opening bracket `(`, `[`, `{` has a correctly typed and correctly ordered closing bracket `)`, `]`, `}`.
- **Stack approach** – push each opener; on each closer, pop and compare against the expected opener from a map.
- **Two failure conditions** – empty stack on a closer means unmatched close; non-empty stack at the end means unmatched opens.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time because each character is pushed and popped at most once; O(n) space worst case.
- **Best practice** – use `ArrayDeque` through the `Deque` interface, not the legacy synchronized `Stack` class.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh at National Bank of India opening nested approval requests. He opens a loan request, then inside it opens a document verification, then a signature request. Each request he writes on a sticky note and places on top of a pile. When a request closes, the one on top must be the most recently opened and the same type. If a signature request tries to close while a document request is on top, the paperwork is rejected.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Validation Walk: "{[()]}"
  ────────────────────────

  Char  Action         Stack (top left)
  ────  ─────────────  ────────────────
  {     push           [ { ]
  [     push           [ [  { ]
  (     push           [ (  [  { ]
  )     pop ( match )  [ [  { ]
  ]     pop [ match ]  [ { ]
  }     pop { match }  [ ]  (empty)

  Stack empty → VALID
```

```text
  Failure Walk: "(]"
  ──────────────────

  Char  Action              Stack
  ────  ──────────────────  ─────
  (     push                [ ( ]
  ]     pop ( expect [ → MISMATCH

  → INVALID
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Parentheses checks whether a string of round, square, and curly brackets is balanced and properly nested. The approach is to scan the string once, push every opening bracket onto a stack, and on every closing bracket pop the top and confirm it is the matching opener using a small map. The two failure conditions are an empty stack when a closer arrives and a non-empty stack after the full scan, and both checks together are what make the solution correct.

The algorithm runs in O(n) time because each character is pushed and popped at most once, with O(n) worst-case space. I always use `ArrayDeque` rather than the legacy `Stack` class because `Stack` extends `Vector` and synchronizes every call, adding pointless overhead. I also add the odd-length shortcut: a string of odd length can never balance, so I reject it before the loop starts.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India, I used this as a fast pre-check on fee-calculation formulas with nested bracket delimiters. A malformed formula is rejected before the expression parser runs, protecting the engine from corrupt input and giving the operations team a clean audit trail of every rejected formula.

The technique extends directly to matching HTML/XML tags, validating nested expressions, and checking balanced quotes in production parsers. The map-based matching makes it trivial to add new bracket types with a single extra entry, so the same validator adapts to any delimiter scheme.

Remember one sentence: push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
